rationale: The Week 2 recorder and the 23-feature detector allowlist implement inter-key latency, key hold time, pointer path length, pointer straightness, and pointer turning entropy. Those five quantities are the standard feature families of keystroke-dynamics and mouse-dynamics research, and the 43-row survey cited none of that literature and contained no source published before 2023. This expansion adds the foundations the implementation already depends on, the classical and behavioural web-bot-detection line that asks the same human-or-machine question on the same signals, the machine-generated-text detection line that supplies the closest cross-modal analogue, and five agent-side sources the project already runs or plans to run but had never surveyed.
selectionRule: A source qualifies if it either (a) defines or benchmarks a feature family that the detector implements, (b) evaluates a human-versus-automation decision using interaction signals rather than content, or (c) is an environment, benchmark, or agent that this repository executes, reproduces, or names as a planned actor.
verificationRule: Every row was resolved to a publisher, ACL Anthology, PMLR, arXiv, or institutional-repository record before entry. Author lists, venues, volume/issue/page numbers, and identifiers were read from that record rather than inferred from citing work.
readStatusPolicy: Read Status is 'Key sections reviewed' only where the primary PDF was opened and specific numbers were taken from it. Sources verified at record and abstract level are recorded as 'Abstract reviewed' and carry a full-text follow-up QA flag.

newTaxonomyValues.note: These values were added because the existing six Paper Type values could not separate a keystroke-dynamics authentication study from an LLM-agent security paper. Both would previously have collapsed into 'Detection / fingerprinting', which is the category the project's own contribution sits in, so that collapse would have hidden the gap this expansion exists to expose.

rows.Title: Keystroke dynamics as a biometric for authentication
rows.Observation/Input: Keystroke latency and duration during typed login and free text
rows.Action Channel: Physical keyboard operated by enrolled human subjects
rows.Agent Architecture: Feature-vector enrollment with distance and probabilistic classifiers
rows.Detection/Defense Target: Verifying claimed user identity from typing rhythm
rows.Benchmark/Dataset: Author-collected typing samples; no shared public benchmark
rows.Metrics: Classification accuracy under varying feature sets
rows.Reproduction Feasibility: Easy: must read/summarize
rows.Key Takeaway: The founding statement of the problem this project inherits: identity, and by extension the human-or-machine question, can be carried by the timing between keystrokes rather than by their content. It also establishes the two primitives the recorder emits, latency between key events and per-key hold duration.
rows.Notes/Blockers: Predates shared benchmarks, so its absolute numbers are not comparable with later work and are not used here. Cited for the feature definition and problem framing only.
rows.Authors: Fabian Monrose; Aviel D. Rubin
rows.Related Seed: Self (feature audit): inter_key_median_ms and key_hold_median_ms in experiments/scienceboard/features.py
rows.Observer Position: Instrumented login client recording key press and release times
rows.Observation Signal: Inter-key latency and key hold duration
rows.Evaluation Setting: Enrolled-user verification against impostor typing samples

rows.Title: User authentication through keystroke dynamics
rows.Observation/Input: Trigraph typing durations over shared text
rows.Action Channel: Physical keyboard operated by 154 enrolled subjects
rows.Agent Architecture: Degree-of-disorder distance over trigraph orderings
rows.Detection/Defense Target: Verifying claimed user identity from typing rhythm
rows.Benchmark/Dataset: 154 subjects typing a shared sample text
rows.Metrics: False alarm rate and impostor pass rate
rows.Reproduction Feasibility: Easy: must read/summarize
rows.Key Takeaway: Introduces a rank-based rather than absolute-time similarity measure, on the argument that typing speed drifts between sessions while the relative ordering of digraph durations is more stable. Reports a false alarm rate near 4 percent with an impostor pass rate below 0.01 percent on 154 subjects.
rows.Notes/Blockers: Uses a fixed shared text, so its stability claim does not automatically transfer to the open-ended simulator tasks used here.
rows.Venue: ACM Transactions on Information and System Security 5(4):367-397
rows.Authors: Francesco Bergadano; Daniele Gunetti; Claudia Picardi
rows.Related Seed: Self (feature audit): inter_key_median_ms in experiments/scienceboard/features.py
rows.Observer Position: Instrumented typing client recording key event times
rows.Observation Signal: Trigraph duration orderings
rows.Evaluation Setting: Fixed shared text typed by 154 enrolled subjects

rows.Title: Keystroke analysis of free text
rows.Observation/Input: Digraph and trigraph timings from unconstrained typed text
rows.Action Channel: Physical keyboard, text freely chosen by the subject
rows.Agent Architecture: Combined absolute-time (A) and relative-order (R) similarity measures
rows.Detection/Defense Target: Continuous identity verification after login
rows.Benchmark/Dataset: Author-collected free-text corpus
rows.Metrics: False alarm rate and impostor pass rate
rows.Reproduction Feasibility: Easy: must read/summarize
rows.Key Takeaway: Moves keystroke dynamics off the fixed password and onto text the subject chooses, which is the regime this project actually operates in. The A-measure plus R-measure combination exists because neither raw speed nor ordering alone survives free-text variation.
rows.Notes/Blockers: Requires per-key identity to form digraphs. The recorder used here deliberately destroys key identity after computing hold time, so this method cannot be applied directly to our traces.
rows.Venue: ACM Transactions on Information and System Security 8(3):312-347
rows.Authors: Daniele Gunetti; Claudia Picardi
rows.Related Seed: doi:10.1145/581271.581272 (User authentication through keystroke dynamics)
rows.Observer Position: Instrumented typing client recording key event times
rows.Observation Signal: Free-text digraph and trigraph latencies
rows.Evaluation Setting: Unconstrained text chosen by each subject

rows.Title: Comparing Anomaly-Detection Algorithms for Keystroke Dynamics
rows.Observation/Input: 31 timing features per password: keydown-keydown, keyup-keydown, and hold times
rows.Action Channel: External keyboard with a reference clock accurate to 200 microseconds
rows.Agent Architecture: 14 re-implemented anomaly detectors evaluated under one shared procedure
rows.Detection/Defense Target: Distinguishing a genuine typist from an impostor typing the same password
rows.Benchmark/Dataset: 51 subjects, 8 sessions of 50 repetitions each, 400 samples per subject, password '.tie5Roanl'
rows.Metrics: Equal-error rate, miss rate, false-alarm rate
rows.Reproduction Feasibility: Easy: public benchmark data and documented procedure
rows.Key Takeaway: The paper exists because the field's published error rates could not be compared: detectors differed in feature set, repetition count, outlier filtering, attempt count, and threshold rule simultaneously. Collecting one dataset and fixing one evaluation procedure moved the three best detectors to equal-error rates between 9.6 and 10.2 percent. This is the methodological precedent for fixing our analysis contract before collection rather than after.
rows.Notes/Blockers: Fixed-password, single-machine, single-keyboard design. Its error rates are not a target for this project; the transferable content is the argument for a pinned protocol and the exact definition of the timing features.
rows.Venue: IEEE/IFIP International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks (DSN 2009):125-134
rows.Evidence Locator: Abstract; Section 2.2 and Table 1; Sections 4.1-4.4; Section 5
rows.Authors: Kevin S. Killourhy; Roy A. Maxion
rows.Related Seed: Self (feature audit): key_hold_median_ms and inter_key_median_ms in experiments/scienceboard/features.py
rows.Observer Position: Dedicated data-collection application with an external reference clock
rows.Observation Signal: Per-key hold time and inter-key latency at sub-millisecond resolution
rows.Evaluation Setting: Repeated fixed-password entry across 8 sessions separated by at least one day

rows.Title: Keystroke Dynamics: Concepts, Techniques, and Applications
rows.Observation/Input: Keystroke timing across fixed-text, free-text, and mobile settings
rows.Action Channel: Physical and touchscreen keyboards
rows.Agent Architecture: Survey of statistical, classical machine-learning, and deep models
rows.Detection/Defense Target: Authentication, continuous verification, and demographic or state inference
rows.Benchmark/Dataset: Surveys public keystroke corpora including the CMU benchmark
rows.Metrics: Equal-error rate and accuracy as reported across surveyed work
rows.Reproduction Feasibility: Easy: read/summarize only
rows.Key Takeaway: Current map of what keystroke timing is known to reveal and how the field now evaluates it. Used here to check that the 2000-2009 foundations cited above have not been superseded in a way that changes the feature definitions the recorder implements.
rows.Notes/Blockers: Surveys human-versus-human identification. It does not cover the human-versus-agent question, which is the gap this project sits in.
rows.Authors: Rashik Shadman; Ahmed Anu Wahab; Michael Manno; Matthew Lukaszewski; Daqing Hou; Faraz Hussain
rows.Related Seed: doi:10.1109/DSN.2009.5270346 (Comparing Anomaly-Detection Algorithms for Keystroke Dynamics)
rows.Observer Position: Literature / lifecycle observer
rows.Observation Signal: Keystroke timing features across the surveyed corpus
rows.Evaluation Setting: Survey of fixed-text, free-text, and mobile keystroke studies

rows.Title: A New Biometric Technology Based on Mouse Dynamics
rows.Observation/Input: Mouse movement speed, direction, travelled distance, and action type
rows.Action Channel: Physical mouse during ordinary desktop session activity
rows.Agent Architecture: Behaviour signature built from binned movement statistics, classified by a neural network
rows.Detection/Defense Target: Continuous identification and intrusion detection from pointer behaviour
rows.Benchmark/Dataset: Author-collected sessions from enrolled users
rows.Metrics: False acceptance and false rejection rates
rows.Reproduction Feasibility: Easy: must read/summarize
rows.Key Takeaway: Establishes the pointer-side feature family this project implements: movement speed against travelled distance, direction histograms, and segmentation of a raw pointer stream into discrete actions. The detector's pointer_speed_px_s and pointer_path_px descend directly from this decomposition.
rows.Notes/Blockers: Requires long observation windows to build a stable signature, which conflicts with our per-task session unit. Sampling rate is not directly comparable to the recorder's 20 Hz pointer throttle.
rows.Venue: IEEE Transactions on Dependable and Secure Computing 4(3):165-179
rows.Evidence Locator: Abstract; behaviour-signature and detector architecture description
rows.Authors: Ahmed Awad E. Ahmed; Issa Traore
rows.Related Seed: Self (feature audit): pointer_path_px, pointer_speed_px_s, pointer_straightness in experiments/scienceboard/features.py
rows.Observer Position: Desktop-session instrumentation capturing global pointer events
rows.Observation Signal: Pointer speed, direction, distance, and action segmentation
rows.Evaluation Setting: Continuous desktop sessions from enrolled users

rows.Title: On mouse dynamics as a behavioral biometric for authentication
rows.Observation/Input: Angle-based metrics over point-and-click pointer curves
rows.Action Channel: Physical mouse performing point-and-click actions
rows.Agent Architecture: Angle-based features with an SVM verifier
rows.Detection/Defense Target: User verification robust to environment and device change
rows.Benchmark/Dataset: Author-collected point-and-click corpus including remote participants
rows.Metrics: Equal-error rate against number of observed clicks
rows.Reproduction Feasibility: Easy: must read/summarize
rows.Key Takeaway: Argues that angle-based descriptors of the movement curve are more stable across machines and environments than raw speed or distance, because they are less sensitive to pointer acceleration settings and screen geometry. This is the direct ancestor of pointer_straightness and pointer_turning_entropy.
rows.Notes/Blockers: Curvature descriptors degrade as sampling rate falls. The recorder throttles pointermove to one sample per 50 ms, which is below the rate typical in this line of work and is an open calibration question for us.
rows.Venue: ACM Symposium on Information, Computer and Communications Security (ASIACCS 2011)
rows.Authors: Nan Zheng; Aaron Paleari; Haining Wang
rows.Related Seed: Self (feature audit): pointer_straightness and pointer_turning_entropy in experiments/scienceboard/features.py
rows.Observer Position: Web-page and desktop instrumentation capturing pointer curves
rows.Observation Signal: Angle-based curvature descriptors of pointer trajectories
rows.Evaluation Setting: Point-and-click tasks across differing machines and environments

rows.Title: User Authentication Through Mouse Dynamics
rows.Observation/Input: Holistic session statistics plus procedural within-movement dynamics
rows.Action Channel: Physical mouse performing a fixed operation task
rows.Agent Architecture: Holistic and procedural feature fusion with one-class classification
rows.Detection/Defense Target: Verifying a user from a short, controlled mouse task
rows.Benchmark/Dataset: Author-collected fixed-task corpus
rows.Metrics: False acceptance rate, false rejection rate, verification time
rows.Reproduction Feasibility: Easy: must read/summarize
rows.Key Takeaway: Separates holistic features, which summarise a whole session, from procedural features, which describe how a single movement unfolds over time. Our current allowlist is almost entirely holistic; the procedural half of this distinction is unimplemented and is the clearest concrete extension available to the detector.
rows.Notes/Blockers: Uses a fixed operation task to control task difficulty. Our simulator tasks are not equalised in that way, so between-task variance is larger here.
rows.Venue: IEEE Transactions on Information Forensics and Security 8(1):16-30
rows.Evidence Locator: Abstract; holistic versus procedural feature definition
rows.Authors: Chao Shen; Zhongmin Cai; Xiaohong Guan; Youtian Du; Roy A. Maxion
rows.Related Seed: doi:10.1109/TDSC.2007.70207 (A New Biometric Technology Based on Mouse Dynamics)
rows.Observer Position: Fixed-task instrumentation capturing full pointer trajectories
rows.Observation Signal: Session-level statistics and within-movement velocity and acceleration curves
rows.Evaluation Setting: Controlled fixed mouse-operation task per subject

rows.Title: Intrusion detection using mouse dynamics
rows.Observation/Input: Raw pointer streams segmented into move, point-and-click, and drag-and-drop actions
rows.Action Channel: Physical mouse during remote administrative sessions
rows.Agent Architecture: Per-action feature extraction with classical classifiers and score aggregation
rows.Detection/Defense Target: Detecting an impostor operating an already-authenticated session
rows.Benchmark/Dataset: Balabit Mouse Dynamics Challenge data set
rows.Metrics: AUC and equal-error rate, reported per action count
rows.Reproduction Feasibility: Medium: public data set; feature pipeline must be rebuilt
rows.Key Takeaway: Provides the action-segmentation recipe, splitting a continuous pointer stream into move, point-and-click, and drag-and-drop units before extracting features, and evaluates on the first widely shared public mouse-dynamics data set. Also shows accuracy rising with the number of observed actions, which bears directly on how long a session must be before our detector should be allowed to decide.
rows.Notes/Blockers: Impostor detection among humans, not human versus agent. Balabit sessions are far longer than our per-task sessions.
rows.Authors: Margit Antal; Elod Egyed-Zsigmond
rows.Related Seed: doi:10.1109/TIFS.2012.2223677 (User Authentication Through Mouse Dynamics)
rows.Observer Position: Session recorder on an administrative remote-access gateway
rows.Observation Signal: Segmented pointer actions with per-action velocity and geometry features
rows.Evaluation Setting: Balabit public benchmark, impostor versus legitimate session

rows.Title: Detecting Automation of Twitter Accounts: Are You a Human, Bot, or Cyborg?
rows.Observation/Input: Posting timing entropy, content features, and account metadata
rows.Action Channel: Platform API and web posting by humans, bots, and mixed accounts
rows.Agent Architecture: Entropy-based timing component plus content and metadata classifiers
rows.Detection/Defense Target: Three-way human, bot, and cyborg account classification
rows.Benchmark/Dataset: Over 500,000 collected accounts
rows.Metrics: Per-class classification accuracy
rows.Reproduction Feasibility: Hard: platform data collection is no longer available on these terms
rows.Key Takeaway: The clearest early statement that human-or-machine is not a binary. Its third class, the cyborg, is an account where automation and a person interleave. Our study has the same latent problem: a human operating a page while an agent holds the tab is neither cleanly human nor cleanly agent, and our labels currently assume it cannot happen.
rows.Notes/Blockers: Signals are posting-level, not input-level, so no feature transfers directly. Cited for the class structure and the timing-entropy argument.
rows.Venue: IEEE Transactions on Dependable and Secure Computing 9(6):811-824
rows.Evidence Locator: Abstract; three-class formulation and measurement scale
rows.Authors: Zi Chu; Steven Gianvecchio; Haining Wang; Sushil Jajodia
rows.Related Seed: Self (label design): human versus agent label vocabulary in experiments/detector/contract.py
rows.Observer Position: Passive platform-side observer of account activity
rows.Observation Signal: Inter-post timing entropy, content, and account metadata
rows.Evaluation Setting: Large-scale observational account corpus

rows.Title: I am Robot: (Deep) Learning to Break Semantic Image CAPTCHAs
rows.Observation/Input: reCAPTCHA risk-analysis signals including browsing history, cookies, and interaction
rows.Action Channel: Automated browser sessions constructed to look legitimate
rows.Agent Architecture: Attack pipeline combining risk-signal manipulation with image classifiers
rows.Detection/Defense Target: Breaking the advanced risk analysis behind image CAPTCHAs
rows.Benchmark/Dataset: Live reCAPTCHA and Facebook image challenges
rows.Metrics: Challenge solve rate and token acquisition rate
rows.Reproduction Feasibility: Easy/Medium: read only; reproduction is ethically and legally constrained
rows.Key Takeaway: Shows the defender's decision is driven by an opaque risk score built from history and interaction signals rather than by the visible puzzle, and that the score can be farmed. Relevant here as the adversarial ceiling: any behavioural detector we build is a risk score, and this is what happens to risk scores once they are worth attacking.
rows.Notes/Blockers: Offensive work against a live production service. Read for the threat model only; we do not attempt any CAPTCHA solving or evasion in this project.
rows.Venue: IEEE European Symposium on Security and Privacy (EuroS&P 2016):388-403
rows.Authors: Suphannee Sivakorn; Iasonas Polakis; Angelos D. Keromytis
rows.Related Seed: arXiv:2103.01748 (Gotta CAPTCHA 'Em All)
rows.Observer Position: External attacker probing a deployed defender's risk score
rows.Observation Signal: Browsing history, cookie age, and interaction signals consumed by the defender
rows.Evaluation Setting: Live deployed CAPTCHA services

rows.Title: Towards a framework for detecting advanced Web bots
rows.Observation/Input: Web server logs together with client-side interaction signals
rows.Action Channel: Scripted and browser-driven web bots at differing sophistication levels
rows.Agent Architecture: Rule-based and machine-learning detection components over combined signals
rows.Detection/Defense Target: Identifying bots that present a legitimate browser fingerprint
rows.Benchmark/Dataset: Author-constructed web bot traffic across sophistication tiers
rows.Metrics: Detection accuracy per bot sophistication tier
rows.Reproduction Feasibility: Medium: paper-first; traffic generation must be rebuilt
rows.Key Takeaway: Sets up the sophistication ladder that the 2021 journal paper then evaluates: bots are not one population, and a detector's accuracy is only meaningful against a stated tier of evasiveness. This is the same reason our leave-one-agent-family-out result matters more than our pooled accuracy.
rows.Notes/Blockers: Superseded in detail by the authors' 2021 DTRAP article, which is the row to read first.
rows.Venue: 14th International Conference on Availability, Reliability and Security (ARES 2019)
rows.Authors: Christos Iliou; Theodoros Kostoulas; Theodora Tsikrika; Vasilis Katos; Stefanos Vrochidis; Ioannis Kompatsiaris
rows.Related Seed: doi:10.1145/3447815 (Detection of Advanced Web Bots by Combining Web Logs with Mouse Behavioural Biometrics)
rows.Observer Position: Website operator combining server logs with page instrumentation
rows.Observation Signal: Request-level log features plus client interaction signals
rows.Evaluation Setting: Constructed bot traffic at moderate and advanced evasiveness

rows.Title: Detection of Advanced Web Bots by Combining Web Logs with Mouse Behavioural Biometrics
rows.Observation/Input: Web log temporal features fused with visitor mouse-movement spatial features
rows.Action Channel: Moderate and advanced web bots driving a real browser
rows.Agent Architecture: Two detection modules, one over web logs and one over mouse movements, combined at the decision level
rows.Detection/Defense Target: Detecting bots that hold a browser fingerprint and imitate humanlike behaviour
rows.Benchmark/Dataset: Author-generated moderate and advanced web bot traffic against an instrumented site
rows.Metrics: Detection performance per bot tier for logs-only, mouse-only, and combined
rows.Reproduction Feasibility: Medium: open-access paper; bot generation and instrumentation must be rebuilt
rows.Key Takeaway: The closest published precedent to this project's design. It fuses a temporal channel with a spatial mouse channel precisely because an advanced bot can forge one but not both, and it reports that the combination is more robust than either module alone against bots built to evade. It also states the operational stake: on the traffic they cite, bots were 37.9 percent of monitored requests.
rows.Notes/Blockers: Its advanced bots imitate humanlike movement by construction. A reasoning CUI agent is not trying to imitate anyone, so it may be an easier or a qualitatively different target; that difference is untested and is a question this project can answer.
rows.Venue: Digital Threats: Research and Practice 2(3), Article 24, 26 pages
rows.Evidence Locator: Abstract; Section 1 introduction and framework rationale; CC-BY open-access copy
rows.Authors: Christos Iliou; Theodoros Kostoulas; Theodora Tsikrika; Vasilis Katos; Stefanos Vrochidis; Ioannis Kompatsiaris
rows.Related Seed: Self (design precedent): combined timing and pointer channels in experiments/scienceboard/features.py
rows.Observer Position: First-party page instrumentation combined with server-side log analysis
rows.Observation Signal: Request timing and sequence features plus mouse-movement spatial features
rows.Evaluation Setting: Instrumented site visited by humans and by two tiers of evasive bots

rows.Title: BeCAPTCHA-Mouse: Synthetic Mouse Trajectories and Improved Bot Detection
rows.Observation/Input: Mouse trajectory coordinates and velocity profiles
rows.Action Channel: Human pointer input versus synthetically generated trajectories
rows.Agent Architecture: Sigma-Lognormal neuromotor decomposition feeding conventional classifiers
rows.Detection/Defense Target: Distinguishing human pointer motion from generated pointer motion
rows.Benchmark/Dataset: BeCAPTCHA-Mouse public benchmark of real and synthetic trajectories
rows.Metrics: Bot detection accuracy against number of observed trajectories
rows.Reproduction Feasibility: Medium: public benchmark released; neuromotor decomposition must be rebuilt
rows.Key Takeaway: Grounds pointer features in a neuromotor model rather than in ad hoc geometry: human movement decomposes into overlapping lognormal velocity strokes, and generated movement generally does not. Offers a principled replacement for our heuristic pointer_straightness, and ships a public benchmark of real and synthetic trajectories.
rows.Notes/Blockers: Its bots are synthesised trajectory generators, not agents driving a browser through a task, so its negative class differs from ours in kind rather than degree.
rows.Evidence Locator: Abstract; neuromotor model and benchmark description; official repository README
rows.Authors: Alejandro Acien; Aythami Morales; Julian Fierrez; Ruben Vera-Rodriguez
rows.Related Seed: Self (feature audit): pointer_straightness and pointer_turning_entropy in experiments/scienceboard/features.py
rows.Observer Position: First-party page instrumentation capturing pointer trajectories
rows.Observation Signal: Trajectory coordinates, velocity profile, and Sigma-Lognormal stroke decomposition
rows.Evaluation Setting: Public benchmark of human and synthetic mouse trajectories

rows.Title: Gotta CAPTCHA 'Em All: A Survey of Twenty years of the Human-or-Computer Dilemma
rows.Observation/Input: Challenge responses, sensor signals, and interaction behaviour across CAPTCHA families
rows.Action Channel: Human and automated responses to active challenges
rows.Agent Architecture: Survey and classification of CAPTCHA schemes and their attacks
rows.Detection/Defense Target: Telling humans from computers at the point of access
rows.Benchmark/Dataset: Surveys deployed and proposed schemes rather than a single corpus
rows.Metrics: Usability, robustness, and reported break rates as surveyed
rows.Reproduction Feasibility: Easy: read/summarize only
rows.Key Takeaway: Twenty years of the same question this project asks, with the field's accumulated conclusion that active challenges get broken and the design pressure moves toward passive behavioural signals. Provides the vocabulary separating active challenge from passive observation, which is the axis our detector sits on.
rows.Notes/Blockers: Predates the LLM-agent wave. Its automation model is scripted or ML solvers, not reasoning agents operating a real browser.
rows.Authors: Meriem Guerar; Luca Verderame; Mauro Migliardi; Francesco Palmieri; Alessio Merlo
rows.Related Seed: doi:10.1109/EuroSP.2016.37 (I am Robot)
rows.Observer Position: Literature / lifecycle observer
rows.Observation Signal: Challenge responses and passive behavioural signals across surveyed schemes
rows.Evaluation Setting: Survey of deployed and proposed human-or-computer schemes

rows.Title: GLTR: Statistical Detection and Visualization of Generated Text
rows.Observation/Input: Per-token probability, rank, and predictive entropy under a reference model
rows.Action Channel: Text generated under several sampling schemes
rows.Agent Architecture: Reference language model scoring with a human-facing visualisation layer
rows.Detection/Defense Target: Helping a person judge whether a passage was machine generated
rows.Benchmark/Dataset: Generated and human passages plus a human-subjects study
rows.Metrics: Human detection rate with and without the tool
rows.Reproduction Feasibility: Easy/Medium: method is simple; reference model needed
rows.Key Takeaway: The earliest of the cross-modal analogues, and the one that frames detection as decision support rather than as an automatic verdict: annotation raised human detection of generated text from 54 to 72 percent without training. Worth holding against the assumption that our detector's output should be a label rather than an explanation.
rows.Notes/Blockers: Different modality entirely. Included as an analogue for how a detection signal is presented and used, not for its features.
rows.Authors: Sebastian Gehrmann; Hendrik Strobelt; Alexander M. Rush
rows.Related Seed: arXiv:2301.11305 (DetectGPT)
rows.Observer Position: Post hoc analyst scoring produced artifacts with a reference model
rows.Observation Signal: Token probability, rank, and entropy
rows.Evaluation Setting: Human-subjects study over generated and human passages

rows.Title: DetectGPT: Zero-Shot Machine-Generated Text Detection using Probability Curvature
rows.Observation/Input: Log-probability of a passage and of its perturbations under a reference model
rows.Action Channel: Text generated by large language models
rows.Agent Architecture: Curvature statistic over perturbed log-probabilities; no trained classifier
rows.Detection/Defense Target: Zero-shot attribution of a passage to a given generator
rows.Benchmark/Dataset: Standard generated-text detection corpora
rows.Metrics: AUROC against supervised and zero-shot baselines
rows.Reproduction Feasibility: Medium: needs reference-model access and perturbation compute
rows.Key Takeaway: Detects generated text without collecting a labelled corpus, by exploiting a structural property of the generator rather than a learned boundary. The parallel worth testing here is whether agent interaction has an equivalent structural signature, which would not require the paired human corpus that our study is otherwise bottlenecked on.
rows.Notes/Blockers: Assumes white-box or near white-box access to the candidate generator. There is no equivalent probability model for a browser interaction trace, so the analogy is conceptual rather than mechanical.
rows.Authors: Eric Mitchell; Yoonho Lee; Alexander Khazatsky; Christopher D. Manning; Chelsea Finn
rows.Related Seed: Self (method design): zero-shot alternatives to a paired labelled corpus
rows.Observer Position: Post hoc analyst with reference-model access
rows.Observation Signal: Log-probability curvature under local perturbation
rows.Evaluation Setting: Generated versus human passages across several source models

rows.Title: A Watermark for Large Language Models
rows.Observation/Input: Token-level membership in a pseudorandomly chosen vocabulary partition
rows.Action Channel: Generation-time sampling modified by the model owner
rows.Agent Architecture: Green-list soft promotion at sampling time with a statistical detector
rows.Detection/Defense Target: Proving machine origin without model access at detection time
rows.Benchmark/Dataset: Author-generated watermarked and unwatermarked text
rows.Metrics: Detection z-score, false positive rate, perplexity cost
rows.Reproduction Feasibility: Medium: reference implementation exists; needs generation control
rows.Key Takeaway: The cooperative alternative to behavioural detection: if the producer marks its own output, detection stops being an inference problem. Directly relevant to the project's framing, because a cooperative agent-side declaration would make our detector unnecessary and an uncooperative one is exactly the case our detector must handle.
rows.Notes/Blockers: Requires the generator's cooperation at sampling time. Nothing analogous exists for pointer and keystroke streams emitted by a third-party agent framework.
rows.Evidence Locator: Abstract; green-list mechanism and detection statistic
rows.Authors: John Kirchenbauer; Jonas Geiping; Yuxin Wen; Jonathan Katz; Ian Miers; Tom Goldstein
rows.Related Seed: arXiv:2301.11305 (DetectGPT)
rows.Observer Position: Cooperating producer marking its own output for later verification
rows.Observation Signal: Token partition membership statistics
rows.Evaluation Setting: Watermarked versus unwatermarked generation at varying entropy

rows.Title: Can AI-Generated Text be Reliably Detected?
rows.Observation/Input: Detector scores under recursive paraphrasing attack
rows.Action Channel: Adversarially paraphrased machine-generated text
rows.Agent Architecture: Attack evaluation plus an impossibility argument over distributional overlap
rows.Detection/Defense Target: Establishing the limits of any generated-text detector
rows.Benchmark/Dataset: Attacks applied to watermarking, zero-shot, and trained detectors
rows.Metrics: AUROC degradation under attack; theoretical AUROC bound
rows.Reproduction Feasibility: Medium: attack is straightforward; full sweep is compute-heavy
rows.Key Takeaway: Bounds the whole enterprise: as the machine and human distributions converge, the best possible detector's AUROC is bounded by their total-variation distance, regardless of method. The honest framing for this project's own claims, and the reason a good result on today's agents should not be reported as a durable capability.
rows.Notes/Blockers: Preprint; the bound is stated for text distributions. Whether interaction traces converge the same way is an empirical question this project does not answer.
rows.Authors: Vinu Sankar Sadasivan; Aounon Kumar; Sriram Balasubramanian; Wenxiao Wang; Soheil Feizi
rows.Related Seed: arXiv:2301.10226 (A Watermark for Large Language Models)
rows.Observer Position: Adversarial analyst attacking deployed detectors
rows.Observation Signal: Detector scores before and after paraphrase
rows.Evaluation Setting: Attack sweep across watermark, zero-shot, and trained detectors

rows.Title: World of Bits: An Open-Domain Platform for Web-Based Agents
rows.Observation/Input: Rendered page pixels, DOM, and reward signal
rows.Action Channel: Low-level keyboard and mouse actions issued into a real browser
rows.Agent Architecture: Reinforcement learning agents over a low-level input action space
rows.Detection/Defense Target: Not a detection paper; defines the task environment
rows.Benchmark/Dataset: MiniWoB task suite and web-scale open-domain tasks
rows.Metrics: Task success rate and reward
rows.Reproduction Feasibility: Medium: MiniWoB descendants are maintained; original platform is dated

rows.Title: GPT-4V(ision) is a Generalist Web Agent, if Grounded
rows.Observation/Input: Screenshots plus HTML structure
rows.Action Channel: Grounded element actions executed on live websites
rows.Agent Architecture: SeeAct: multimodal planning followed by an explicit grounding stage
rows.Detection/Defense Target: Not a detection paper; supplies a planned experimental actor
rows.Benchmark/Dataset: Mind2Web offline plus a live-website online evaluation
rows.Metrics: Task success rate offline and online, per grounding strategy
rows.Reproduction Feasibility: Medium/Hard: live sites drift and a multimodal model endpoint is required
rows.Key Takeaway: Separates planning from grounding and shows the gap between them is where web agents fail: GPT-4V completed 51.1 percent of live tasks when its textual plans were manually grounded. For this project the relevant consequence is that the grounding stage is what emits the actual click and type events, so an agent's trace signature is shaped by its grounding strategy rather than by its reasoning.
rows.Notes/Blockers: Named as a planned ScienceBoard actor in this repository but never previously surveyed. Recorded here to close that gap before any formal run.
rows.Evidence Locator: Abstract; grounding-strategy comparison; official project page

rows.Key Takeaway: The multi-environment comparison the survey was missing, and the source of the observation that agent competence varies far more across environments than across tasks within one.
